title: A Monkey's Silvery Fur May Explain Its Link to a Moon God
summary:
In ancient Egypt, Thoth was the god of wisdom, magic, and the moon. He was shown as two animals: a black-and-white bird called the African sacred ibis, and a silvery monkey called the hamadryas baboon. Why the baboon? A new study says its color may be the answer. Its fur closely matches the color of the moon. The findings appeared in the journal Time and Mind on July 14.

Nathaniel Dominy, a scientist who studies primates at Dartmouth College, wanted to solve this puzzle. Baboons eat farmers' crops in parts of Africa, and they do not come from Egypt. Egyptians brought them in as special pets. Egyptologist Julien Cooper found that Thoth's name comes from a word meaning 'bright' and 'white,' like moonlight.

Dominy and Cat Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews used a tool called a spectrometer to measure light bouncing off baboon hairs at the American Museum of Natural History. The hamadryas fur matched moonlight exactly, and it was about 65 percent brighter than olive baboon fur. The scientists think the baboons reminded Egyptians of moonlight.
why_it_matters: It shows how looking closely at animals can help solve puzzles from thousands of years ago.
